title: Antenatal Care & the Antenatal Clinic
description: The role of antenatal care, routine clinic checks, the healthcare team, and screening and diagnostic tests in pregnancy.
content_html:
What is Antenatal Care?

Antenatal care is the programme of appointments, tests and health guidance offered to pregnant women from early in their pregnancy until they go into labour. In the UK, care is co-ordinated by the NHS and is free of charge. The goals of antenatal care are to monitor the health of both mother and baby, identify and manage any complications as early as possible, prepare parents for labour and birth, and provide emotional support and health education. Women are encouraged to register with their midwife or GP as soon as they believe they are pregnant, ideally before 10 weeks, to ensure they receive the full schedule of appointments and first-trimester screening.

The Booking Appointment

The first formal antenatal appointment is known as the booking appointment and ideally takes place between 8 and 10 weeks of pregnancy. It is usually conducted by a midwife and typically lasts an hour or more. At the booking appointment, the midwife will: take a full medical history (including any previous pregnancies, chronic conditions and current medications); check the woman's blood pressure; test a urine sample for protein (which can indicate pre-eclampsia or infection), glucose (to screen for gestational diabetes) and bacteria; take blood to determine blood group, rhesus factor, haemoglobin level (to detect anaemia), and to screen for conditions including HIV, syphilis, hepatitis B and rubella immunity; calculate the due date (estimated date of delivery) from the last menstrual period; and discuss lifestyle factors including diet, exercise, smoking and alcohol.

At subsequent routine appointments, the same checks — blood pressure, urine, and from 24 weeks onwards, fundal height (measuring the growth of the uterus with a tape measure) — are repeated at every visit to track progress and detect any changes. From around 28 weeks, the midwife will also feel the baby's position (palpation) and check the foetal heartbeat using a handheld Doppler device.

Key Fact

Blood pressure is monitored at every antenatal appointment because raised blood pressure (hypertension) in pregnancy can indicate pre-eclampsia — a serious condition that, if untreated, can restrict the baby's growth, cause organ failure in the mother, and become life-threatening. Early detection allows treatment to begin before the condition becomes dangerous.

The Antenatal Healthcare Team

Several healthcare professionals may be involved in a woman's antenatal care, depending on whether her pregnancy is low-risk or requires specialist input. The midwife is the lead professional for most low-risk pregnancies, providing continuity of care from booking through to the postnatal period. The GP (general practitioner) often refers women for antenatal care, manages any ongoing medical conditions during pregnancy, and may carry out some routine appointments. The obstetrician is a hospital-based consultant who takes over or shares care when pregnancies are classified as high-risk — for example, if the mother has diabetes, high blood pressure, a multiple pregnancy (twins or more) or a history of complications. Other professionals involved can include the anaesthetist (for epidurals or caesarean sections), a diabetic specialist midwife (for gestational diabetes), a physiotherapist (for pelvic girdle pain) and, where relevant, neonatologists who specialise in the care of premature or sick newborns.

Ultrasound uses high-frequency sound waves to create images of the developing baby inside the womb without using radiation. In the UK, two routine scans are offered to all pregnant women. The dating scan (also called the 11-13 week scan) confirms the pregnancy is in the uterus, accurately establishes the due date, checks for a heartbeat and can detect multiple pregnancies. As part of this scan, the nuchal translucency measurement — the thickness of the fluid-filled space at the back of the baby's neck — is taken and combined with blood test results to calculate the statistical risk of chromosomal conditions such as Down's syndrome, Edwards' syndrome and Patau's syndrome. This is a screening test, not a diagnostic one: a high-risk result does not confirm a condition but indicates that a diagnostic test should be offered. The anomaly scan at around 20 weeks checks the baby's physical development in detail, looking at the brain, heart, kidneys, spine, face, limbs and placenta position, and can identify structural abnormalities such as spina bifida or heart defects.

Diagnostic Tests: Amniocentesis and CVS

Where screening tests indicate a higher risk of a chromosomal or genetic condition, diagnostic tests can be offered to give a definitive answer. Amniocentesis is carried out from around 15 weeks. Under ultrasound guidance, a fine needle is passed through the mother's abdomen to draw a small amount of amniotic fluid, which contains foetal cells. The cells are cultured and the chromosomes examined. Results typically take one to three weeks. Chorionic villus sampling (CVS) is an alternative performed earlier (10-13 weeks), in which a small sample of placental tissue is taken; it carries a similar or marginally higher miscarriage risk to amniocentesis — approximately 0.5% (1 in 200) for both procedures when performed by a skilled operator, according to current NHS and RCOG guidance — but provides results more quickly.

Both amniocentesis and CVS are offered (not required) to women who receive a high-risk screening result, who are over 35, or who have a known family history of a chromosomal or genetic condition. Because both carry a small risk of miscarriage, the decision to accept or decline a diagnostic test is a personal one that midwives and genetic counsellors support without pressure. A positive result gives parents certainty about the baby's condition and allows them to prepare, seek further specialist care, or make decisions about the pregnancy.

Key Fact

Amniocentesis is a diagnostic test carried out from around 15 weeks of pregnancy. A fine needle is used to withdraw a small sample of amniotic fluid containing foetal cells, which are tested for chromosomal conditions such as Down's syndrome. It carries an approximate miscarriage risk of up to 0.5% (1 in 200) according to current NHS guidance, and provides a definitive result, unlike screening tests which only indicate risk level.

A screening test (e.g. the nuchal translucency scan and combined blood test) gives a risk level — for example ‘1 in 50 risk of Down's syndrome’ — but cannot confirm whether the baby has the condition. A diagnostic test (amniocentesis or CVS) analyses the baby's own cells and gives a definitive result. In exam answers, never say a screening test ‘confirms’ or ‘diagnoses’ a condition — this is inaccurate and will cost marks. Use the word ‘indicates’ or ‘estimates the risk’ for screening, and ‘confirms’ only for diagnostic tests.
exam_tip_html: Questions on antenatal care often ask you to ‘describe the role of’ a specific professional. Always match the professional to the correct setting and type of pregnancy: midwife = lead care for low-risk pregnancies; obstetrician = high-risk or complicated pregnancies in a hospital setting; GP = referral and management of ongoing conditions. For questions comparing screening and diagnostic tests, use the terms ‘indicates risk’ for screening and ‘confirms/diagnoses’ for diagnostic tests, and always include the miscarriage risk when discussing amniocentesis or CVS.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Antenatal care begins at the booking appointment (8-10 weeks) and includes routine checks at every visit — blood pressure, urine testing and fundal height — to monitor the health of mother and baby and detect complications early.
  • The antenatal healthcare team includes the midwife (lead for low-risk pregnancies), GP (referral and chronic conditions) and obstetrician (high-risk or complicated pregnancies); other specialists are involved as needed.
  • Screening tests such as the nuchal translucency scan estimate the risk of chromosomal conditions but cannot confirm them; diagnostic tests such as amniocentesis analyse the baby's actual cells to give a definitive result but carry a small risk of miscarriage.

glossary_terms.definition: The healthcare and support provided to a pregnant woman from conception to the start of labour, designed to monitor the health of mother and baby and identify any complications early.
A qualified healthcare professional who provides care and advice to women throughout pregnancy, labour and the postnatal period.
A doctor who specialises in pregnancy, labour and conditions affecting the female reproductive system, taking lead care in high-risk pregnancies.
A diagnostic prenatal procedure in which a small sample of amniotic fluid is withdrawn from the sac surrounding the baby using a fine needle, allowing the baby's chromosomes to be analysed.

practice_questions.text:
Which professional typically leads antenatal care for a low-risk pregnancy in the UK?
A) Obstetrician
B) GP
C) Midwife
D) Health visitor
State two checks that are carried out at every routine antenatal appointment.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any two from: blood pressure check / urine test (for protein, glucose, bacteria) / weight check / fundal height measurement (from 24 weeks) / foetal heartbeat (from later appointments) / foetal position check (palpation). Both must be distinct. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain the difference between a screening test and a diagnostic test in antenatal care.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: a screening test identifies risk level / indicates whether further testing is needed. 2 marks: screening cannot confirm whether a condition is present — it gives a statistical risk (e.g. a 1 in 100 chance of Down's syndrome). 3 marks: a diagnostic test such as amniocentesis analyses the baby's actual chromosomes and gives a definitive yes or no answer, but carries a small risk of miscarriage (approximately 0.5%, or 1 in 200, per current NHS guidance), unlike screening tests which are risk-free to the baby. [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe the role of the obstetrician in antenatal care. Give one example of a situation where an obstetrician would take the lead.
practice_questions.marks: Role (up to 2 marks): an obstetrician is a hospital-based doctor specialising in pregnancy and birth who takes over or shares care when a pregnancy is classified as high-risk; they monitor and manage complications and may plan or carry out medical interventions such as a caesarean section (2 marks for a clear, developed description; 1 mark for a basic statement). Example (up to 2 marks): for example, if a woman develops gestational diabetes or pre-eclampsia, the obstetrician takes the lead in managing her care, as these conditions can threaten the lives of both mother and baby and require specialist treatment (2 marks for a specific, applied example; 1 mark for a vague example). [4 marks total]

practice_questions.text:
A pregnant woman at 12 weeks receives a result from her combined screening test showing a 1 in 30 risk of Down's syndrome. Her midwife offers her an amniocentesis.

Discuss the factors the woman should consider when deciding whether to have the amniocentesis.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6 marks): A balanced discussion covering: the benefit of a definitive result (the amniocentesis will confirm or rule out Down's syndrome, allowing informed planning and access to specialist support); contrasted with the miscarriage risk (approximately 0.5%, or 1 in 200), the emotional stress of the procedure and the wait for results, and the fact that a high-risk screening result does not mean the baby definitely has the condition (1 in 30 means a 97% chance the baby does not). The discussion should acknowledge the non-directive nature of the decision.
Secure (3–4 marks): Two relevant factors explained with some reference to the scenario.
Developing (2 marks): One factor with a brief reason.
Emerging (1 mark): A single point with no development. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
A community midwifery team is reviewing its booking appointment process after data showed that 20% of women in the area were registering for antenatal care after 12 weeks.

Evaluate the importance of early registration for antenatal care and the consequences of late booking for the health of mother and baby.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7–8 marks): A balanced evaluation arguing that early registration (ideally by 10 weeks) allows first-trimester screening (nuchal scan, combined blood test) to be completed in time, enables early detection of conditions such as ectopic pregnancy, pre-eclampsia risk factors and anaemia, and gives time for lifestyle interventions. Counter-argument: late booking does not inevitably lead to poor outcomes — many complications can still be identified and managed in the second trimester, and the most damaging complications (e.g. neural tube defects) are influenced by pre-conception health rather than booking timing. Structural barriers to early booking (e.g. women unsure of pregnancy, access issues, language barriers) should be acknowledged. A clear, substantiated judgement is required.
Secure (5–6 marks): At least two well-developed points with an attempt at a judgement.
Developing (3–4 marks): Relevant points but one-sided.
Emerging (1–2 marks): Basic points with no evaluation. [8 marks]

knowledge_checks.q: What does a urine test check for at routine antenatal appointments?
Which type of test gives a definitive diagnosis of a chromosomal condition such as Down's syndrome?
In the UK, the dating scan is offered at approximately _____ weeks of pregnancy.
An obstetrician takes the lead in antenatal care when a pregnancy is classified as _____.
Match each antenatal test to its correct description.
right: Checks baby's physical development and organ structure at around 20 weeks
Withdraws amniotic fluid to test baby's chromosomes; diagnostic
Confirms due date and checks nuchal translucency at 11-13 weeks

flashcard_questions.q: When does the booking appointment ideally take place?
What does the nuchal translucency measurement assess?
flashcard_questions.a: The statistical risk of chromosomal conditions such as Down's syndrome.

flashcard_questions.q: What is pre-eclampsia and what routine check detects it?
flashcard_questions.a: A serious pregnancy condition causing raised blood pressure, detected at every antenatal appointment.

flashcard_questions.q: At approximately what week is the anomaly scan carried out?
What does the anomaly scan check?
flashcard_questions.a: The baby's physical development, including brain, heart, kidneys, spine, face, limbs and placenta position.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the approximate miscarriage risk associated with amniocentesis?
flashcard_questions.a: Up to approximately 0.5% (1 in 200) per current NHS guidance.

flashcard_questions.q: From what week is fundal height measured at antenatal appointments?
What blood group information is taken at the booking appointment and why is rhesus factor important?
flashcard_questions.a: Blood group and rhesus factor are checked; rhesus-negative mothers may need anti-D injections to prevent harm to the baby.
A diagnostic test at 10-13 weeks where placental tissue is sampled to check the baby's chromosomes.

flashcard_questions.q: What condition does gestational diabetes screening detect?
flashcard_questions.a: High blood glucose during pregnancy, which can affect the baby's growth and health.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the role of the GP in antenatal care?
flashcard_questions.a: To refer women for antenatal care, manage ongoing medical conditions and carry out some routine appointments.

flashcard_questions.q: What does a high-risk combined screening result mean?
flashcard_questions.a: It indicates an increased statistical risk of a chromosomal condition, not a confirmed diagnosis.
